newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition, Socialists plan rival councils.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition, Socialists plan rival councils.

text.p: Serbia's opposition, vowing to keep up protests against election fraud, headed on Tuesday for a confrontation with ruling Socialists as both sides prepared to form rival councils in a provincial town.

The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition said it planned to swear in its councillors at a ceremony on Tuesday morning outside the city hall in the town of Smederevska Palanka, some 80 km (50 miles) southeast of the capital Belgrade.
The Socialists meanwhile were expected to swear in their version of the municipal council -- with a Socialist party majority -- inside the building.
Zajedno said its actions were based on the results of the November local elections, which were later overturned by Socialist authorities.
Zajedno said it won a majority of 26 seats out of 49 in the local election but a court later ruled the Socialists had won 25 and Zajedno 24 seats.
The rival ceremonies would heighten the risk of violent confrontation and raised the possibility of parallel governments in other towns where Zajedno's victories were overturned, including Belgrade.
Zajedno has led 10 weeks of street demonstrations that have turned into calls for an end to autocratic rule by President Slobodan Milosevic and his powerful wife.
Tens of thousands turned out in Belgrade for a religious procession on Monday led by the traditionally pro-government Serbian Orthodox Christian church.
The church patriarch broke his initial silence and has sided with students backing opposition demands for the recognition of the municipal poll results.

Zajedno said on Monday it lost a legal battle over Belgrade voting when a district court dismissed appeals from an electoral commission and upheld earlier rulings rejecting an opposition victory in the city.

Electoral commission chairman Radomir Lazarevic was enraged by the decision which he described as purely political. "The decision is completely against the law...Truth and justice are endangered," he said.

Analysts said the court decision may have closed any possibility for further appeals and could set the stage for a political showdown in which Zajedno and the Socialists would attempt to form rival city governments in Belgrade.
The United States, which has led Western criticism against election fraud, denounced the court decision as "a step in the wrong direction".

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington the international community and a majority of the Serbian people believed that the opposition had won in Belgrade "freely and fairly".
Washington condemned Belgrade authorities for loosening the leash on riot police who had begun to take a tougher line against the daily protests.

Since the protests started in November, Milosevic has tried to stifle them with a hostile state media campaign, piecemeal concessions, delaying tactics, police force and an invitation to an international fact-finding mission.
The opposition protests, marked by an irreverent, merry atmosphere, have won Western support and show no sign of flagging despite winter cold and creeping police violence.
Experts with the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) invited by Milosevic ended up endorsing opposition claims of victory in the country's 14 biggest towns.
Zajedno leaders, pledging to keep up the protests, said time was on their side and that Milosevic's burden was growing every day the street demonstrations continued.
